newsitem.title: USA: Double therapy best for some lung cancers - study.
newsitem.headline: Double therapy best for some lung cancers - study.

text.p: Patients with a certain form of lung cancer who get both chemotherapy and radiation therapy appear to live longer those given only radiation therapy, a study announced on Tuesday says.

The finding applies to non-small-cell lung cancers that have advanced locally but have not spread throughout the body. About one-third of the 170,000 cases of lung cancer diagnosed in the United States each year are non-small-cell.

The study, to be published on Wednesday in the Journal of the National Cancer Institute, followed 155 patients. Although neither group lived long, the 78 patients who received both forms of treatment lived a median of 13.7 months, while the other 77 patients lived 9.6 months.

After two years, survival rates were 26 percent for the combined-therapy group and 13 percent for the radiation group. In a six-to-seven-year follow-up, 13 percent of the combination group had survived vs. 6 percent of the radiation group.

If all patients with this form of cancer received combined therapy, an additional 5,100 might live at least five years, the researchers -- led by Dr. Robert Dillman of the Hoag Cancer Centre of Newport Beach, California -- concluded.

But in an accompanying editorial, Dr. David Johnson of Vanderbilt University Medical School in Nashville, Tennessee, said it was too soon to apply the study across the board. Physicians must make individual evaluations of which approach is better for specific patients, he said.
